title: Water rocket 2: fins and stability
summary: Build small and large fins for the water rocket, check stability with a swing test, and see which set flies straighter.
materials: the water rocket launcher and bottles from week 5
cardstock or foam board for fins

steps.title: Ask, imagine, plan
steps.body:
The design loop continues: ask, imagine, plan, build, test, fix.

Ask: last week's rocket sometimes tipped over sideways in the air. What decides whether a rocket flies straight or tumbles?

Imagine: two points on the rocket. One is where its weight balances, called the centre of mass. The other is where the air pushes back on it hardest, called the centre of pressure. A rocket flies straight when its centre of mass sits ahead of its centre of pressure, toward the nose.

Plan: cut two sets of fins from cardstock or foam board, one small and one large, sized so they attach the same way to the bottle. Sketch where you expect each set to move the centre of pressure.

figure.alt: A rocket body shown upright with a nose cone and two tail fins. A dot marks the centre of mass higher up, near the nose; another dot marks the centre of pressure lower down, near the fins. A caption explains that when the nose tips sideways, the fins push the tail back in line because the centre of pressure sits behind the centre of mass.

items.s: CM ahead of CP flies straight
Nose tips: fins push the tail back straight

steps.title: Nose heavy flies straight
steps.body:
A rocket's centre of mass is the single point where all its weight balances, found by resting it on one finger until it sits level. Its centre of pressure is the point where the air's push effectively acts as it moves through the air. Fins move that point backward, toward the tail, and bigger fins move it further back.

A rocket is stable when its centre of mass sits ahead of its centre of pressure. Then, if the nose tips sideways, the air pushes harder on the tail than the nose. That push swings the tail back in line, the nose leading the way like a weathervane.

A rocket with its centre of pressure ahead of its centre of mass does the opposite: any tip gets worse instead of correcting, and it tumbles. Bigger fins, placed near the tail, are usually the fix, since they pull the centre of pressure further back.

figure.alt: A rocket hangs from a string tied at its centre of mass, held by a hand above, with its nose cone up and two tail fins at the bottom. A caption explains that in the swing test, a stable rocket keeps its nose leading the whole way round the circle.

items.s: Swing test: nose should lead all the way round
Nose leads the whole way round = stable

steps.title: Swing test, then launch
steps.body:
Balance each finished rocket, small fins and large fins, on one finger to find its centre of mass, and mark it. Tie a loop of string around that point and, in a clear outdoor space away from people, swing the rocket gently overhead in a circle.

A stable rocket points its nose in the direction it is moving the whole way round. A rocket that tumbles or trails nose-first is not stable yet, and needs bigger fins or a heavier nose before it is worth launching.

Launch each stable design three times, with the same water volume and pump strokes as week 5's best result. An adult operates the release, and everyone wears safety glasses and stands well back. After each landing, measure the straight-line distance from directly under the launch point to where it landed.
checklist: Each rocket's centre of mass was found and marked before the swing test
The swing test was done in a clear space away from people
Both fin sizes passed the swing test before either one was launched
Each fin size was launched three times with the same water volume and pump strokes
Everyone wore safety glasses and stood well back while the adult operated the release

steps.title: Fin size versus landing distance
steps.body:
The water volume, the pump strokes and the launcher stay the same for every row. Only the fin size changes.

Launch each fin size three times, six rows in total. For each flight, write the fin size and how far it landed from directly under the launch point, in metres.
steps.question: Which fin size landed closer to directly below the launch point, and by about how many metres?

steps.title: Bug diary
steps.body:
One line for each thing that did not work the first time and what you tried. Classics this week: fins taped on unevenly, so the rocket veers the same direction every launch no matter how stable it swings.

Also watch for a swing test done too gently to tell tumbling from a genuine wobble, and a landing distance measured from the wrong starting point.

steps.title: Show it
steps.prompt: Photo of the swing test for both fin sizes, plus your table of the six landing distances
